HEADLINE: Goldman in AES corner
INTRO: United States-based AES Corporation has wasted no time finding an adviser for its run at IFM Investors' Pacific Hydro.
TEXT:
United States-based AES Corporation has wasted no time finding an adviser for its run at IFM Investors' Pacific Hydro.

As Bank of America Merrill Lynch and Credit Suisse market the hydro and wind renewable energy assets to potential buyers, it's understood the New York-listed AES has drafted in investment bank Goldman Sachs.

The mandate comes as banks across Australia and North America seek to sign mandate letters ahead of the formal information memorandum's release in August and indicative bids in September.

As Street Talk reported last week, the sell-side advisers have told potential bidders that Pacific Hydro had a 1.8 gigawatt total development pipeline in hydro and wind.

PacificHyrdro expects $175 million earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the 2015 calendar year, on a normalised basis, with 52 per cent coming from Chilean assets, 41 per cent from Australia and the balance in Brazil.

HEADLINE: The next Pillar in Baird's privatisation push
INTRO: NSW Treasury Corp is quietly readying to offload its superannuation support business Pillar Administration.
TEXT:
NSW Treasury Corp is quietly readying to offload its superannuation support business Pillar Administration.

It is understood a trade sale is the more likely exit route than an initial public offering, with potential buyers including the soon-to-be-floated Link Group.

Deutsche Bank completed a scoping study into the potential sale of Pillar in November 2013, at the behest of Premier Mike Baird, after the company put its hand up for a $30 million cash injection to fund a technology upgrade.

In the 2014 budget the state coughed up $7 million to kick-start the project, and now Pillar is asking for a $15 million instalment to complete the next phase.

Pacific Equity Partner's upcoming $2.5 billion-plus Link IPO has raised awareness in the market of how much money there is to be made from clipping the ticket on super payments.

Link Group is a roll-up of 35 businesses. One of its most successful deals has been the turnaround of Superpartners, which it acquired last year from five major industry funds - AustralianSuper, Cbus, HESTA, HOSTPLUS and MTAA Super.

That deal added 4.7 million accounts to Link's super administration business.

Pillar's two main clients are NSW public sector funds First State Super and State Super. It manages a combined total of around 1 million accounts.

The sale of Pillar is likely to be one of the least controversial items on the expenditure review committee's asset recycling agenda, which has previously run the ruler over more public facing assets such as divisions of the water board.

Baird has certainly cemented NSW's status as the business-friendly state, with the government's $9 billion TransGrid sale off and running.

Information memorandums are being examined by seven heavyweight consortiums, while the Victorian government struggles to get its Port of Melbourne privatisation under way and Queensland battles with an $80 billion debt pile, after it kyboshed $30 billion-plus worth of asset sales.

HEADLINE: HSBC serious about Aussie M&A, hires UBS's Couzner
INTRO: HSBC has signalled it is serious about claiming a piece of the local advisory market, hiring a former UBS banker and creating a new role as head of mergers and acquisitions in Australia.
TEXT:
HSBC has signalled it is serious about claiming a piece of the local advisory market, hiring a former UBS banker and creating a new role as head of mergers and acquisitions in Australia.

Ex-UBS banker Scott Couzner has been appointed as HSBC's head of M&A in Australia, reporting to Asia Pacific M&A boss Jason Rynbeck and locally to head of capital financing Sean Henderson.

Couzner was most recently head of M&A for South-East Asia at UBS.

It's understood the hire comes as HSBC seeks to take a bigger piece of the growing local advisory pie.

Australia-targeted M&A is up by 10 per cent over the past year to $US56.8 billion, with inbound activity accounting for 46 per cent of the total.

HSBC sees an opportunity in the Australian market to utilise its global presence, while having more troops on the ground locally will also help service existing clients. HSBC has already made some headway this year, jagging a buy-side role on the NSW government's $9 billion TransGrid privatisation.

HSBC has close links with China's State Grid and is advising the state-owned utility's consortium on TransGrid, along with Macquarie Capital. State Grid has teamed up with Macquarie Group's Macquarie Infrastructure and Real Assets.

Elsewhere, short positions in Bellamy's Australia have been building in the lead-up to the organic food and beverage company's full-year result. Around $81 million worth of stock will be released from escrow three days after the numbers are handed down.

Bellamy's has been a star performer, surging by close to 400 per cent since its July initial public offering, and driving strong returns for initial investors including AMP Capital, Ellerston Capital and Regal Funds Management.

HEADLINE: Riverside portfolio in peak condition with IPAR purchase
INTRO: Australia's ageing population and growing levels of healthcare spending have driven lucrative returns for investors in recent years.
TEXT:
Australia's ageing population and growing levels of healthcare spending have driven lucrative returns for investors in recent years.

And staying healthy has been a winning theme before for global private equity firm The Riverside Company in Australia. It made a handsome profit with its purchase and exit from Boost Juice, and now it's making a return.

This time it's more of a pure healthcare business, one that helps people get back to work after they've done their back or have been temporarily slowed down with carpal tunnel syndrome after hitting the keyboard too ferociously in the office.

Street Talk can reveal Riverside has invested in IPAR Rehabilitation, a Melbourne-based firm which delivers occupational rehabilitation case management services.

IPAR services big insurers who administer or underwrite the workers' compensation cases for a whole host of government arms. It's a national firm with its shingle out in 41 locations around the nation, and with about 240 staff.

The deal comes at a time when healthcare spending is growing by 8 per cent a year.

Industry players speculated to Street Talk that IPAR would have plenty of upside for producing organic growth or buying complementary businesses and integrating them. Its business Cogent Thinking which works in the outsourcing of injury claims management is a logical place to expand.

Riverside, which hired Nick Speer as a principal in May 2014, has also been active in the education space, with a bolt-on acquisition for Learning Seat.

This asset is based in Melbourne and was acquired in 2012 by the private equity firm, which is led in Australia by Simon Feiglin.

Elsewhere in private equity, TPG-owned Alinta is now planning to shut down its two power stations near Port Augusta in South Australia by March, 2017, having pulled forward the closure by 12 months after stunning the locals a few weeks ago with the news that it was all over and that 400-plus jobs would go.

Finally, sources told Street Talk on Thursday night The Carlyle Group was weighing a retreat from ANZ Banking Group's Esanda Dealer Finance auction.

While the private equity behemoth was yet to officially pull the pin, well-placed sources are questioning its commitment to the sale process.

Carlyle's withdrawal would leave Macquarie's Corporate and Asset Finance division and China's HNA Group still in the race.

HEADLINE: Airportlink's $69m pitch to Transurban rivals
INTRO: Up-for-sale Brisbane tollroad Airportlink may be a high margin and highly efficient asset, which could see more traffic as competing roads become more congested. But it is almost impossible to see how any bidder could stop Transurban from adding Airportlink as the sixth and final piece of its Queensland portfolio.
TEXT:
Up-for-sale Brisbane tollroad Airportlink may be a high margin and highly efficient asset, which could see more traffic as competing roads become more congested. But it is almost impossible to see how any bidder could stop Transurban from adding Airportlink as the sixth and final piece of its Queensland portfolio.

Airportlink advisers Fort Street Advisers and Macquarie Capital kicked off Airportlink's sale on Thursday morning, with the release of a teaser document to potential buyers introducing the road and its financial metrics.

The 6.7 kilometre road was expected to record $55 million earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the 2015 financial year, increasing to as much as $69 million in 2016.

The flyer, obtained by Street Talk, said an average 51,577 vehicles used the road each day in the June quarter and 85.5 per cent of users during the 2015 financial year were passenger vehicles.

It said Airportlink's current owner, the bankrupt BrisConnections, owned the road's concession until July 30, 2053, which means any new owner get the asset for 38 years.

Importantly, the road cost $3.2 billion to build and is now expected to be worth about $1 billion. Even under the most aggressive sale forecasts - and using IFM Investors' eye-popping purchase of Indiana Toll Road at 32-times EBITDA in March as an example - the road would be worth $1.76 billion.

The flyer pitched Airportlink as a best-in-class road with high margins, stable operational and earnings performance and a favourable earnings outlook. It said the road had highly efficient tolling and back office systems and there was scope to renegotiate or amend and extend the operations and maintenance contract in the near term.

And it also flagged the network development opportunities.

But you have to wonder how any interested and rational party could out-bid Transurban. The $19 billion Australian owns concessions to Brisbane's five other tollroads and would have synergies across back office, tolling and maintenance which could never be matched by another bidder.

Transurban is known to be interested and has appointed UBS to advise on the bid, as Street Talk reported on May 1. Flagstaff and Macquarie, working on behalf of receiver PPB Advisory, are expected to target those parties which missed out on the now Transurban-owned Queensland Motorways portfolio to get a competitive auction under way.

HEADLINE: Flaw in credit assessment standards to be revealed
INTRO: An official review of lending standards in the red-hot investor property market is set to reveal serious flaws in how lenders have been assessing customers for credit.
TEXT:
An official review of lending standards in the red-hot investor property market is set to reveal serious flaws in how lenders have been assessing customers for credit.

The chairman of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, Greg Medcraft, on Thursday said the watchdog would in August publish a report finding shortcomings among how some lenders were testing borrowers' ability to cope with higher interest rates.

The report, based on surveillance of 11 banks and non-banks, had also found some lenders' credit checks used inadequate estimates of customers' living expenses, he said.

Even though banks are offering new borrowers interest rates of about 4.5 per cent, Mr Medcraft lenders and customers needed to assess whether borrowers could cope with interest rates of 7 per cent.

"That's what you should be thinking about if you're looking at your ability to repay the loan," he said.

But adding to similar concerns raised by the prudential regulator in recent months, Mr Medcraft said the report had made "mixed" findings on whether banks were using a high enough "stress rate."

He added that some of the underwriting standards had been improved in recent months. "Many of them have since corrected their ways or are correcting them." Mr Medcraft also highlighted some borrowers failing to rigorously assess a borrowers' cost of living, including national indexes that did not reflect local variations.

"Some are using a cost of living index that is completely inappropriate for where that person is living. So if they're living somewhere like Paddington in Sydney, probably using the poverty line as the cost of living for that person is probably inappropriate."

The findings come after banks have been forced to tighten their lending to housing investors in response to official concerns of excessive risk-taking in the $1.3 trillion mortgage market.

ANZ Bank, Commonwealth Bank and National Australia Bank and AMP Bank have all lifted interest rates for housing investors since last Thursday, a move they have justified by pointing to a 10 per cent a year cap in investor credit growth.

Speaking at a lunch in Melbourne, NAB chief executive Andrew Thorburn said he was alert to the risks in market but NAB also needed to serve customers who were in a strong financial position. "We feel pretty comfortable with the risk we are taking on. We don't disagree that we need to be prudent at this point in the cycle but we also need to acknowledge there are real customers out there that have can actually deliver against not just the interest rate we are giving them, but against 7 per cent, which is the minium rate that we put into the system," Mr Thorburn said.

Mr Medcraft also joined other regulators in urging customers to be wary of the risks created by very low interest rates, stressing that people needed to think about managing their loan repayments a more 'normal' environment."

"The whole issue at the moment in the markets is you've got to get people appreciating we are in a unusual situation, there's an extraordinary amount of liquidity," Mr Medcraft said.

Reserve Bank governor Glenn Stevens told the same conference it was hard to know in advance whether stricter rules on banks would prevent another crisis however regulators had little choice but to boost capital buffers.

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority has also highlighted flawed lending standards from lenders in recent months - though it does not regulate lenders that do not take deposits from customers.

Mr Medcraft, who previously worked in securitisation markets, said failure to have proper underwriting standards could lead to serious problems.

"Frankly as I saw in the United States and elsewhere, this is where often the issue is, when underwriting is compromised," he said.

Various banks have bolstered their credit checks of customers in recent months, while ASIC also named Bank of Queensland as one bank that had moved to apply more rigorous assessment of borrowers' living expenses.

Banks have responded to the risks in housing - and APRA's 10 per cent speed limit - by cutting discounts for investors, forcing borrowers to stump up bigger deposits, and assessing incomes more stringently.

This week AMP Bank also took the more drastic step of freezing new lending to housing investors so that it does not breach the cap.

It can't be known whether the higher levels of capital being imposed on banks will be sufficient to protect the financial system from another crisis, says Reserve Bank governor Glenn Stevens.

But he said the measures, which are being introduced in Australia and around the world to reduce bank leverage and create bigger equity buffers to absorb losses, were not likely to do the economy any harm.

HEADLINE: NAB's focus on growing business lending division pays off
INTRO: National Australia Bank chief executive Andrew Thorburn says the company has its "confidence back" as it returns to growth in its crucial small and medium business banking division, and works through the sale of its problem US and UK assets.
TEXT:
National Australia Bank chief executive Andrew Thorburn says the company has its "confidence back" as it returns to growth in its crucial small and medium business banking division, and works through the sale of its problem US and UK assets.

NAB is Australia's biggest business bank. Since his appointment in April last year, Mr Thorburn has made the division a priority, adding 200 bankers to try to win back market share.

He said business lending growth was at about 6 per cent and in NAB's core market of business clients, with up to $100 million turnover, it was again growing in line with the broader market and no longer losing share.

"We are growing at system in that market, which we weren't 12 or 18 months ago. So we are back there, and we are happy about that," he said on Thursday.

"It's not like with mortgages. Business clients are hard won, and when you start to lose your core business client, that is not good. I think we've stabilised that. I don't think today we are delivering the best service and all the capabilities we need but I think we're far stronger," Mr Thorburn said.

He said the bank was also delivering on its promise to exit its banks in the US and UK. NAB sold the last tranche of its Great Western bank in the US this week but chief financial officer Craig Drummond admitted the demerger of the British bank Clydesdale had been complicated by a shifting regulatory landscape. "It's proceeding as expected but ... it's complex and the UK budget was unhelpful for us."

The UK government has introduced an 8 per cent tax on bank profits and removed a controversial bank levy. But the demerger is on track for the end of the year and Mr Thorburn said shareholders have supported the move, announced at the same time as NAB's plan to raise $5.5 billion in capital.

"I don't think we would have raised that capital so quickly if they didn't back our strategy."

Mr Thorburn and Mr Drummond said NAB was comfortable with its levels of capital in light of the push from the Australian Prudential Regulatory Authority to increase the capital through both changes to risk weightings on mortgages.

Mr Drummond said any further capital requirements necessitated by new international rules on capital would come with a lengthy transition period.

But Mr Thorburn warned bank investors would need to share the burden of any capital increases. He said it's unlikely that Australian banks' returns on capital, at 15 to 20 per cent, will be sustainable.

Mr Thorburn also reaffirmed his commitment to NAB's struggling wealth management business, arguing it was important to retain clients. "If it's done well, it's a really important part of the product suite for our clients. If we don't have it, there is a risk that those clients start to go somewhere else and we lose some of the banking business."

But he said NAB would look at exiting parts of the wealth business where margins were low and scale was difficult to build. "I think we have to look with more intensity at some bits we think don't fit. But we think wealth, particularly simple insurance and simple super, are things we want to be in."
